opus-5.5.text:
I think of autonomous driving as a kind of older sibling to robotics. In a sense, a self-driving car *is* a robot: it perceives the world, makes decisions, and acts in the physical world. But it's a very particular kind of robot, with a fairly constrained action space. You're mostly controlling steering, throttle, and brake, and the goal is actually to *avoid* contact with everything around you.

Robotics, especially manipulation, is almost the opposite. The whole point is to make contact with the world: to pick things up, push, fold, insert, use tools. Once you start touching things, the physics gets much harder. You have friction, deformable objects, uncertainty about mass and geometry, and the action space becomes high-dimensional. So while driving is about navigating *through* the world, manipulation is about *changing* the world, and that's a fundamentally harder capability to acquire.

That said, I think the two fields have a lot to teach each other. Autonomous driving went through a whole arc: first the modular pipeline era, with hand-engineered perception, prediction, and planning, and then a gradual shift toward more end-to-end, data-driven approaches as companies accumulated huge fleets and huge amounts of driving data. A lot of what we're seeing in robotics now feels like an echo of that. People are asking: can we collect enough data, can we scale up models, can we get generalization the way driving and language models did?

The big difference is the data. Driving had a natural data flywheel. Millions of people already drive every day, and you can put sensors on those cars. Robotics doesn't have that. Nobody is out there doing household manipulation with a robot arm at scale. So we have to think much harder about where data comes from: teleoperation, simulation, human videos, or new hardware that makes collection cheaper. In many ways that's the central question of the field right now.

There's also a lesson about timelines and humility. Driving showed us that getting a demo working is one thing, but getting to the long tail of reliability is a whole different game, and it took far longer than people expected. I think robotics will face the same thing, perhaps even more so, because the diversity of tasks and environments is so much larger. So I see them as very connected. Driving is a preview of the challenges, and in some ways a proof that this kind of learning-based approach can eventually work in the real world. But robotics is pursuing a broader and, in some sense, deeper kind of physical intelligence.

It does not identify earlier robotics path-planning and control approaches as aligning with approaches some autonomous-driving companies pursue today.

r002.rationale: The response describes robotics as pursuing broader physical intelligence and learning-based approaches, but does not characterize it as exploring a paradigm beyond traditional path planning and control or describe the fields as running parallel tracks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest way to put it is that autonomous driving is a special case of robotics, but it's a special case that got industrialized first, and that changes how the two fields relate to each other.

A self-driving car is a robot with one task, a very constrained action space, and an environment that, while open-world, is actually fairly structured. There are lanes, traffic rules, other agents who mostly behave predictably. So autonomous driving was the first place where we could ask the full question, perception, prediction, planning, control, all in a real-world loop, with real safety consequences, at scale. And the field got pulled forward by enormous capital and very clear economics. That meant a lot of the engineering infrastructure, data pipelines, simulation, fleet learning, safety validation, got built out there years before general robotics had anything comparable.

General robotics is the harder problem by an order of magnitude. The action space is much bigger, you have contact, manipulation, deformable objects, and the environments are far less standardized. A kitchen is much messier than a highway. So for a long time, robotics looked like the field that was always ten years away, while driving looked like the field that was almost there.

What's changed recently is that the direction of influence is starting to reverse. The big shift in driving over the last few years was moving from modular pipelines to end-to-end learned systems, where you train from sensor input to action and let the model absorb the intermediate representations. That lesson came out of driving partly because driving had the data. But the same recipe, large models, lots of embodied data, learning the whole stack, is now the central bet in general robotics, and robotics is starting to generate ideas that feed back, things like how you build foundation models that transfer across embodiments, how you deal with the long tail when you can't drive a million miles to collect it.

So I'd say they're pursuing the same capability, which is intelligent action in the physical world, but they're attacking it from opposite ends. Driving started narrow and deep, with one task done to safety-critical reliability. Robotics is starting broad and shallow, with many tasks at a demo level, trying to climb toward reliability. And I think the interesting question for the next few years is where they meet. My guess is that the people who've shipped a driving stack have a much better intuition for what reliability actually costs, and the people in robotics have a much better intuition for what generality requires. Neither side has both yet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses autonomous driving’s shift from modular pipelines to end-to-end learning, but does not identify an alignment with earlier robotics path-planning and control approaches.

r002.rationale: It describes driving and robotics as starting from opposite ends and influencing each other, but does not say that robotics’ move beyond traditional path planning and control makes them resemble parallel tracks.

astra-6.text:
I see autonomous driving as a particular form of robotics. In both cases, you’re trying to build a machine that can perceive its surroundings, decide what to do, and act in the physical world. The important part is that those abilities form a loop: every action changes what the machine encounters next.

But the constraints are different. A car has a relatively narrow set of actions—steer, accelerate, brake—yet it has to handle an enormous range of situations with very high reliability. A general-purpose robot may move more slowly, but it has to deal with many more kinds of interaction: grasping an object, opening a door, or working around a person.

So I think the fields can learn a lot from each other, without assuming that progress transfers automatically. Autonomous driving pushes us to think seriously about safety, uncertainty, and operating at scale. Broader robotics pushes us toward more flexible physical capabilities. The shared challenge is turning an impressive demonstration into something you can depend on.

r002.rationale: The response compares the fields’ constraints and potential to learn from each other, but does not describe robotics exploring a paradigm beyond traditional path planning and control or characterize the fields as parallel tracks.

sol-6.1.text:
I see autonomous driving as a particular form of robotics. In both cases, a machine has to perceive its surroundings, predict what might happen, decide what to do, and act in the physical world. So they share a lot of underlying challenges.

But their constraints are different. A car has a relatively narrow set of actions—steering, accelerating, braking—yet it has to operate reliably in an open environment, alongside people whose behavior it cannot control. A general-purpose robot may need a much broader range of physical skills, especially manipulation, where contact and small errors can change the situation completely.

The relationship is productive because progress can flow both ways. Autonomous driving pushes capabilities in perception, prediction, simulation, and building reliable systems. Robotics broadens the questions: how do you learn new tasks, interact with objects, and adapt when the environment changes? I think the shared ambition is to connect intelligence with action, but success in one setting does not automatically solve the other.
